title: Łódź: A City Built by Its Jewish Community
summary: This article explains the scale and breadth of Jewish life in Łódź before the destruction, from economic activity to communal institutions.
editorialContent:
## From a small town to an industrial center

The story remembered in the memorial book is not simply that Jews lived in Łódź, but that they helped make its urban life: its businesses, schools, associations, religious institutions and political culture. The book evokes “life in Łódź” and “the Jews of Łódź,” and recalls a community that grew with the city’s transformation. Its three accounts emphasize different aspects—social and cultural life, the community’s great size, and its educational and welfare institutions—rather than giving one single chronology. Together, they describe a community whose importance reached far beyond its numbers. ([Community of Łódź](/communities/lodz/records/mention_7cf21187ba458875fe942af7); [Jewish community of Łódź](/communities/lodz/records/mention_359e7216d59a25e03734a45f); [Jews of Łódź](/communities/lodz/records/mention_f3cb15f27be5748231c78657))

That growth began in a very different place from the manufacturing metropolis Łódź would become. Virtual Shtetl traces Jewish settlement to the late eighteenth century, naming a baker, Daniel Layzerowicz, and a tailor, Abram Lewkowicz, among the earliest recorded Jewish residents. In 1793, it reports, only 11 of the town’s 190 inhabitants were Jewish. By the early nineteenth century, as Łódź’s population expanded, Jewish residents were organizing communal life. The community’s first recorded elections took place in 1810; in 1811 its elders arranged land for a cemetery and established a burial society. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/497-lodz/99-history/137633-history-of-community?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book recalls Łódź as “Polish Manchester,” a name that captures the city’s industrial transformation. It also remembers Jews and Germans as a substantial part of the population and describes Jewish participation in the city’s economic life. But the book’s phrasing is not a census table: it gives a community’s retrospective understanding of its place in the city. For a statistical check, Virtual Shtetl reports that in 1921 Łódź had 156,155 Jewish residents—34.5 percent of its population—making it one of Poland’s largest Jewish centers after Warsaw. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/tradycja-i-kultura-zydowska/historia-zydow-w-polsce/najbardziej-zydowskie-miejsca-w-polsce?utm_source=openai))

## Institutions for a growing community

Industrial growth drew people to Łódź and created a need for institutions that could serve a large, diverse population. The memorial book remembers a first Jewish school, an Agudath school and a small yeshiva, alongside educational, medical, childcare and eldercare services. These were not incidental additions to the city’s Jewish population: they helped sustain communal life across generations, meeting needs that employment and family networks alone could not meet. The book’s account of a “nearly quarter-million” community expresses the scale remembered by survivors, while the US Holocaust Memorial Museum gives a prewar figure of more than 233,000 Jews. The figures are close, but they should not be treated as interchangeable: they come from different records and may reflect different dates or ways of counting. ([First Jewish school in Łódź](/communities/lodz/records/mention_bbd2205881769f240d5b65c5); [Łódź Jewish community](/communities/lodz/records/mention_359e7216d59a25e03734a45f); [USHMM: Łódź](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lodz)) ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lodz?utm_source=openai))

Religious life also changed with the city. The memorial book remembers the [Lodzer Synagogue](/communities/lodz/records/mention_940b868f2ea5f64d7137a3a9) as one of Europe’s finest. Independent local-history research adds a longer architectural history: Virtual Shtetl documents a communal synagogue built in 1809, when Łódź was still a small town, and describes the later Altshtot synagogue as a major building in the old Jewish quarter. These institutions reflect more than a rising population. They show how communal resources, religious practice and urban identity developed together. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/497-lodz/112-synagogues-houses-of-prayer-and-others/86855-first-communal-synagogue-lodz-ul-dworska-currently-wolborska?utm_source=openai))

The book also preserves a more contested side of civic life. It describes Jewish students and graduates excluded from an organization, and recalls cooperation between Jews and Germans that lasted until Nazi influence reached Łódź. It names Isaac Grinbaum as a prominent Polish Jewish political figure and notes a Jewish printers’ union, founded by 1906 before tsarist authorities closed it. Such memories point to a community participating in public and economic life while facing discrimination and political limits. The supplied account does not identify the organization that excluded Jewish graduates, so its precise identity remains an open question. ([Jewish-German political cooperation](/communities/lodz/records/mention_6bb1003d2b1202b17ba6c827); [Lodz Jewish Printers Union](/communities/lodz/records/mention_45d9138e83439eb7f25c8e69); [Isaac Grinbaum](/communities/lodz/records/mention_d9eccad49460d98b719ede7c))

## The city’s rupture

Łódź’s Jewish life was never separate from the city’s wider population. The memorial book remembers Jews, Germans, Poles and Russians within a changing urban setting, while its account also describes how German occupation and local participation in persecution broke the ties of ordinary city life. The book names Poles described as Volksdeutsche in the process of isolating Jews. That testimony belongs to the memorial book; it should not be generalized into a claim about all Polish residents. ([Poles](/communities/lodz/records/mention_b901b760694d70a97f2ee7dc); [Germans](/communities/lodz/records/mention_5f8b8e47acd13213f1f341fa); [Russians](/communities/lodz/records/mention_d3f72187645a4e824d82ce5f))

The outside historical record establishes the scale and mechanics of the rupture. German forces occupied Łódź in September 1939, and the Germans established a ghetto in early 1940, forcing Jewish residents into a confined district. The USHMM describes the city as a major textile center before the war and the ghetto as a site of forced production for German industry. This was a violent distortion of the older relationship between Jewish life and Łódź’s economy: industrial skill and labor, once part of a shared urban world, were seized and exploited under occupation. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lodz?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book remembers the Jewish community council being shot by Germans, and later speaks of the ghetto and Auschwitz through the language of loss and survival. The USHMM’s account supplies the broader chronology: mass deportations from the ghetto, its liquidation in 1944, and the deportation of most remaining residents to Auschwitz-Birkenau. These are not the same kind of evidence. The book conveys what survivors chose to remember about their city and its people; the museum record situates those memories within the documented machinery of persecution and murder. ([Łódź Ghetto](/communities/lodz/records/mention_08f6bb20f4ea7d0def1f031b); [Auschwitz](/communities/lodz/records/mention_0b13dec1e28fc5b4544a392d); [USHMM: Destruction of the Łódź Ghetto](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1942-1945/liquidation-of-the-lodz-ghetto)) ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1942-1945/liquidation-of-the-lodz-ghetto?utm_source=openai))

## What the community built—and what remains to ask

To say that Łódź was built by its Jewish community is not to say Jews alone built it. The city’s industrial rise involved many groups, and the memorial book itself remembers a mixed population. Its more precise claim is that Jewish residents were not marginal to Łódź’s development: they built institutions, entered industries, organized politically and culturally, and helped shape the city’s character. The community’s destruction therefore altered not only Jewish life but the history of Łódź itself.

The memorial book’s testimony is indispensable, but it is not a complete register of everyone connected to the city. Its survivor-authors could not tell the whole story of those who emigrated, died elsewhere, or survive only in other archives. Further research could identify the organization that excluded Jewish graduates, trace the printers’ union’s members, and establish how the book’s remembered community figures relate to census dates. The city’s history is richer when its intimate testimony is read alongside institutional records—and when unanswered questions remain visible.
